title: Linux Essentials
subtitle: Jeopardy Review

jeopardyFormatExample.clueText: The command that prints the absolute path of your current working directory

categoryLegend: Files & Directories: pwd, cp -r, find, ln -s.  Text Processing & Pipes: grep, sed, awk, pipes, redirection.  Users, Groups & Permissions: chmod, chown, umask, SUID, sudo.  Packages & Software: apt, dnf, dpkg, rpm.  Processes, Services & Scheduling: ps, systemctl, journalctl, cron.  Networking & Storage: ip, ss, /etc/fstab, LVM, df.

clues.clue: The command that prints the absolute path of your current working directory.
clues.explain: pwd stands for 'print working directory' and outputs the full path from the filesystem root to your current location. It is one of the first navigation commands taught in any Linux course.

clues.clue: The cp flag that preserves file metadata — timestamps, ownership, and permissions — during a copy operation.
clues.explain: cp -p (preserve) copies a file while keeping its original modification time, access time, ownership, and permission bits intact. Without -p, the copy receives the current timestamp and the invoking user's umask-derived permissions.

clues.clue: The find option that searches for files larger than 50 megabytes, written in find's size syntax.
clues.explain: find uses -size with a suffix (c=bytes, k=kilobytes, M=megabytes, G=gigabytes) and a + prefix to mean 'greater than'. For example: find /var -size +50M locates files exceeding 50 MB under /var.

clues.clue: Unlike a symbolic link, this type of link shares the exact same inode number as the original file and cannot span different filesystems.
clues.explain: A hard link created with ln (no -s flag) is a second directory entry pointing to the same inode — the same block of actual data on disk. Because it references an inode number, it must live on the same filesystem as the original.

clues.clue: The stat field that shows how many hard links currently point to a file's inode, which drops to zero only when the file's data blocks are freed.
clues.response: What is the link count (or Nlink)?
clues.explain: Every inode tracks a link count: each hard link increments it, each removal decrements it. The kernel only releases the data blocks when the link count reaches zero and no process holds the file open. stat displays this as 'Links:' in its output.

clues.clue: The pipe character that takes the standard output of one command and feeds it as standard input to the next.
clues.explain: The vertical bar | connects commands in a pipeline so the stdout of the left command becomes the stdin of the right command. For example, ls -l | less pages through a long directory listing.

clues.clue: The grep flag that makes a pattern search case-insensitive, so 'error', 'ERROR', and 'Error' all match.
clues.explain: grep -i performs a case-insensitive match, treating uppercase and lowercase letters as equivalent. This is useful when log files mix capitalization conventions unpredictably.

clues.clue: This redirection operator appends standard output to the end of an existing file rather than overwriting it.
clues.explain: Using >> (double greater-than) opens the target file in append mode, so new output is added after the last existing byte. A single > truncates the file first, which can cause accidental data loss.

clues.clue: The sed command that, in-place, replaces every occurrence of the word 'foo' with 'bar' on all lines of a file named data.txt.
clues.explain: The -i flag tells sed to edit the file in-place (modifying it directly). The substitution expression s/foo/bar/g uses the g flag to replace all occurrences on each line, not just the first.

clues.clue: The file descriptor numbers for standard input, standard output, and standard error, respectively.
clues.explain: Every Linux process inherits three open file descriptors: 0 (stdin), 1 (stdout), and 2 (stderr). Redirection operators target these numbers — for example, 2>/dev/null silences error output by redirecting fd 2 to the null device.

clues.clue: The numeric UID that always belongs to the root account on a Linux system.
clues.explain: The kernel grants superuser privileges based on UID 0, not on the username 'root'. Any account assigned UID 0 has full administrative access, regardless of what it is named.

clues.clue: The chmod numeric mode that gives the owner read/write/execute, the group read/execute, and others read/execute.
clues.explain: In octal notation each digit sums r=4, w=2, x=1: owner 4+2+1=7, group 4+0+1=5, others 4+0+1=5. This mode is the standard for publicly executable files and directories.

clues.clue: The file that stores hashed user passwords and is readable only by root on modern Linux distributions.
clues.explain: /etc/shadow was introduced to move password hashes out of the world-readable /etc/passwd file. It is typically owned by root with mode 000 or 640, preventing ordinary users from accessing the hashes.

clues.clue: The default umask value on most Linux systems, and the resulting default permissions it produces for newly created regular files.
clues.explain: The umask is subtracted from the maximum new-file permission of 666: 666 minus 022 equals 644 (rw-r--r--). For directories the maximum is 777, so 777 minus 022 equals 755.

clues.clue: The special permission bit, represented by a leading 4 in the octal mode (e.g., 4755), that causes an executable to run with the file owner's privileges rather than the caller's, used by /usr/bin/passwd.
clues.response: What is the SUID (Set User ID) bit?
clues.explain: When the SUID bit is set on an executable, the kernel temporarily elevates the running process's effective UID to match the file owner's UID. /usr/bin/passwd needs this because it must write the root-owned /etc/shadow.

clues.clue: The apt command used on Debian/Ubuntu to install a package named 'tree'.
clues.explain: apt install downloads the named package and its dependencies from the configured repositories, then unpacks and configures them. It should typically be preceded by apt update to refresh the local package index.

clues.clue: On RHEL and Fedora systems, this command has replaced yum as the recommended high-level package manager.
clues.explain: DNF (Dandified YUM) is the default package manager for Fedora 22+ and RHEL/CentOS 8+. It offers better dependency resolution, improved performance, and a Python 3 code base compared to the older yum.

clues.clue: The key difference between a high-level package tool like apt or dnf and a low-level tool like dpkg or rpm regarding dependencies.
clues.response: What is that high-level tools automatically resolve and install dependencies, while low-level tools do not?
clues.explain: dpkg and rpm install only the package file given to them; if a dependency is missing the install fails with an error. apt and dnf consult repository metadata to find and install all required packages automatically.

clues.clue: The dpkg flag used to list all files installed on the system by a package — for example, to see every file provided by the 'curl' package.
clues.explain: dpkg -L packagename prints every file that was unpacked from that package's .deb archive. The related flag -S (or --search) does the reverse: given a file path it shows which package owns it.

clues.clue: The optional RHEL/CentOS repository that provides thousands of additional open-source packages not included in the base distribution, commonly enabled with 'dnf install epel-release'.
clues.response: What is EPEL (Extra Packages for Enterprise Linux)?
clues.explain: EPEL is maintained by the Fedora Project and provides packages that are available in Fedora but absent from RHEL and its clones. Enabling it gives administrators access to tools like htop, the fish shell, and many others.

clues.clue: The ps command and flags that show all running processes on the system in a detailed, user-oriented format.
clues.explain: ps aux (BSD-style flags without a dash) displays every process regardless of controlling terminal (a), shows processes owned by other users (u), and includes processes not attached to any terminal (x). The output includes PID, CPU, memory, and command.

clues.clue: The systemctl subcommand that both starts a service immediately AND configures it to start automatically at the next boot.
clues.explain: systemctl enable creates the symlink that adds the unit to the appropriate target's wants directory (enabling it at boot), while the --now flag also starts it immediately in the current session. Without --now you need a separate systemctl start.

clues.clue: In a crontab entry, this five-field sequence runs a script every day at 2:30 AM: the fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week.
clues.explain: The cron time fields in order are minute (0-59), hour (0-23), day of month (1-31), month (1-12), and day of week (0-7, where 0 and 7 are Sunday). Asterisks mean 'every valid value', so 30 2 * * * fires at 02:30 every day.

clues.clue: The journalctl flag combination that shows only log entries from the current boot that have a priority of 'error' or worse.
clues.explain: -b (or --boot) restricts output to the current boot session, and -p err (or --priority=err) filters to entries at severity level 3 (error) and higher — that is, errors, critical, alert, and emergency messages.

clues.clue: The systemd target that corresponds to traditional runlevel 3 — a fully operational multi-user environment with networking but no graphical display server.
clues.explain: systemd replaces SysV runlevels with named targets. multi-user.target provides a complete network-capable, multi-user text environment analogous to runlevel 3. graphical.target (runlevel 5) adds the display manager on top of it.

clues.clue: The iproute2 command used to display all IP addresses currently assigned to every network interface on a Linux system.
clues.response: What is ip addr (or ip addr show)?
clues.explain: ip addr is the modern replacement for the deprecated ifconfig command. It lists every interface along with its assigned IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, subnet masks, and state. The iproute2 suite (ip, ss) ships with all major distributions.

clues.clue: The local file that maps hostnames to IP addresses and is checked before DNS queries on most Linux systems.
clues.explain: /etc/hosts is a static lookup table; entries take the form 'IP hostname'. The order in which the system consults hosts versus DNS is controlled by /etc/nsswitch.conf, but the default puts 'files' (i.e., /etc/hosts) before 'dns'.

clues.clue: The lsblk-family command that displays block devices, their sizes, mount points, and partition layout in a tree format.
clues.explain: lsblk reads /sys/block and presents disks, partitions, and LVM logical volumes in an easy-to-read tree. It shows device names (sda, sdb), sizes, type (disk/part/lvm), and where each is mounted without requiring root.

clues.clue: The three LVM commands executed in sequence to build the logical volume layer: one prepares a physical disk partition, one creates a volume group from it, and one carves out a logical volume.
clues.response: What are pvcreate, vgcreate, and lvcreate?
clues.explain: LVM uses a three-layer abstraction: pvcreate initializes a block device as a Physical Volume, vgcreate combines one or more PVs into a Volume Group, and lvcreate allocates a Logical Volume from the VG's pooled space. The LV is then formatted and mounted like any partition.

clues.clue: The reason administrators prefer to use a filesystem's UUID rather than its device name (like /dev/sdb1) in /etc/fstab.
clues.response: What is that UUIDs are persistent and unique, while device names can change between boots?
clues.explain: Linux assigns block device names (sda, sdb, nvme0n1) based on probe order, which can shift when hardware is added or removed. A UUID is embedded in the filesystem superblock and never changes, guaranteeing /etc/fstab mounts the correct partition after any hardware reconfiguration.
